suspending or cancelling a person’s driver 
licence (including a conditional licence) lies 
ultimately with the driver licensing authority.
Licensing decisions are based on a full 
consideration of relevant factors relating to 
health and driving performance.

For a conditional licence to be issued, the 
health professional must provide to the 
driver licensing authority details of the 
medical criteria not met, evidence of the 
medical criteria met, as well as the proposed 
conditions and monitoring requirements.

While a person may meet individual disease 
criteria, concurrent medical conditions

for example, hearing, visual or cognitive 
impairment (refer to Part A section 2.2.7.

Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness exists when 
a person does not regularly sense the usual 
early warning symptoms of mild hypoglycaemia 
such as sweating, tremulousness, hunger, 
tingling around the mouth, palpitations and 
headache. It markedly increases the risk of a 
severe hypoglycaemic event occurring and is 
therefore a risk for road safety. Rates of severe 
hypoglycaemia may be up to seven times higher 
compared with those who retain hypoglycaemia 
awareness. Impaired hypoglycaemia awareness 
occurs in 20–25 per cent of people with type 
1 diabetes and about 10 per cent of those with 
type 2 diabetes. Prevalence is higher in older 
people and in those with a longer duration

defined in section 3.2.1. Hypoglycaemia), the 
person should not drive for a significant period

The minimum period of time before returning 
to drive is generally six weeks because it often 
takes many weeks for patterns of glucose

driving period will depend on factors such

patient’s behaviour and objective measures of 
glycaemic control (documented blood glucose) 
over a reasonable interval. 
Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness 10–14
Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness exists when 
a person does not regularly sense the usual 
early warning symptoms of mild hypoglycaemia 
such as sweating, tremulousness, hunger, 
tingling around the mouth, palpitations and 
headache. It markedly increases the risk of a 
severe hypoglycaemic event occurring and is 
therefore a risk for road safety. Rates of severe 
hypoglycaemia may be up to seven times higher 
compared with those who retain hypoglycaemia 
awareness. Impaired hypoglycaemia awareness 
occurs in 20–25 per cent of people with type 
1 diabetes and about 10 per cent of those with 
type 2 diabetes. Prevalence is higher in older 
people and in those with a longer duration 
of diabetes."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-457570d561f8a4dd", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-457570d561f8a4dd | Patient Survey", "node_id": "0033", "section": "3.2.4", "pdf_page": 108, "original_text": "Patient Survey

Neuropathy and foot care
While it can be difficult to be prescriptive

important that the severity of the condition is 
assessed. Adequate sensation and movement

Sleep apnoea
Sleep apnoea is a common comorbidity 
affecting many people with type 2 diabetes and 
has substantial implications for road safety. The 
treating health professional should be alert to 
potential signs (e.g. BMI greater than 35) and 
symptoms, and apply the Epworth Sleepiness 
Scale as appropriate (refer to section 8. Sleep 
disorders).

{"module": "blackout", "licence_context": "commercial", "query": "Synthetic nurse note for software testing. No real patient data.

The nurse reviews a commercial driver's symptoms alongside information from a witness, the treating team and an older workplace form, because each source describes a different part of the story; the occupational record retains those differences and identifies completed current findings without turning a booking, a family account or a recollection into a measured patient result.

A signed specialist review confirms a single blackout of undetermined nature after completed investigations, no recurrent blackout and an event-free interval of 7 years; appropriate specialist information is available for the commercial assessment, whereas the driver's recollection of feeling light-headed during a recent blood draw is explicitly documented as preserved awareness rather than another blackout, so it is not added to the confirmed event count.

The employer's copied form relates to an earlier period of work and contains a broad satisfactory box without the measurements underlying it, whereas the current nurse entry identifies the source of each specific finding; the driver's wish to continue scheduled duties is recorded as a preference, not as proof that the present assessment has resolved the documented concern.

The nurse keeps the relevant current attachment with the record and identifies the older account by its timing, so a later reviewer can distinguish what was observed, what the driver reported and what remains unresolved; no additional measurement, specialist conclusion or diagnosis is added merely because it would make the occupational decision easier to complete.

{"module": "blackout", "licence_context": "commercial", "query": "Synthetic nurse note for software testing. No real patient data.

At a scheduled commercial-driver medical, the driver answers questions in several stages because a dispatcher keeps calling about the next route, while the nurse checks a current clinical document against a copied workplace summary; an observation described confidently in conversation is kept separate from a finding actually recorded in an identified examination.

The specialist's signed history confirms two blackouts separated by more than 24 hours, with the last event 7.5 years ago and the mechanism still undetermined after completed investigations; the driver has had no more recent confirmed events, but the two episodes were not merely clustered in one day, and a family account that calls them one illness does not change the documented separation or the elapsed interval.

The usual work involves coupling trailers, checking mirrors, interpreting radio messages and responding to pedestrians in a loading area, with breaks that can be delayed when deliveries run late; the driver explains which difficulty occurred while stationary and which was noticed during ordinary duties, rather than claiming that quiet conversation in the clinic reproduces every task in the cab.

The nurse also records possible hearing loss after repeated missed spoken instructions, and audiometry has not been performed; the driver can follow a quiet conversation but no unaided better-ear threshold, complete frequency set or qualified aided-performance result is available for this separate screening concern.

The record is prepared for the reviewing clinician with the sequence of events and the provenance of the available findings intact, because the employer summary and the driver's account answer different questions; a completed test is retained as such, but an unresolved detail is not filled in from a family member's history or from an earlier document with different testing conditions.

{"module": "blackout", "licence_context": "commercial", "query": "Synthetic nurse note for software testing. No real patient data.

At a scheduled commercial-driver medical, the driver answers questions in several stages because a dispatcher keeps calling about the next route, while the nurse checks a current clinical document against a copied workplace summary; an observation described confidently in conversation is kept separate from a finding actually recorded in an identified examination.

The specialist's signed history confirms two blackouts separated by more than 24 hours, with the last event 7.5 years ago and the mechanism still undetermined after completed investigations; the driver has had no more recent confirmed events, but the two episodes were not merely clustered in one day, and a family account that calls them one illness does not change the documented separation or the elapsed interval.

The usual work involves coupling trailers, checking mirrors, interpreting radio messages and responding to pedestrians in a loading area, with breaks that can be delayed when deliveries run late; the driver explains which difficulty occurred while stationary and which was noticed during ordinary duties, rather than claiming that quiet conversation in the clinic reproduces every task in the cab.

The nurse also records possible hearing loss after repeated missed spoken instructions, and audiometry has not been performed; the driver can follow a quiet conversation but no unaided better-ear threshold, complete frequency set or qualified aided-performance result is available for this separate screening concern.

The record is prepared for the reviewing clinician with the sequence of events and the provenance of the available findings intact, because the employer summary and the driver's account answer different questions; a completed test is retained as such, but an unresolved detail is not filled in from a family member's history or from an earlier document with different testing conditions.

{"module": "vision", "licence_context": "commercial", "query": "Synthetic nurse note for software testing. No real patient data.

At a scheduled commercial-driver medical, the driver answers questions in several stages because a dispatcher keeps calling about the next route, while the nurse checks a current clinical document against a copied workplace summary; an observation described confidently in conversation is kept separate from a finding actually recorded in an identified examination.

The driver sometimes notices vehicles late on the left and brings a field printout marked 140 degrees, but its reliability flag is poor and the treating optometrist has not confirmed a defect or a valid horizontal extent; central letters seem clear to the driver, no complete specialist interpretation is attached, and the nurse records the symptoms and the unreliable test separately rather than converting either into a confirmed static visual field disorder.

The employer's copied form relates to an earlier period of work and contains a broad satisfactory box without the measurements underlying it, whereas the current nurse entry identifies the source of each specific finding; the driver's wish to continue scheduled duties is recorded as a preference, not as proof that the present assessment has resolved the documented concern.

The nurse reads the summary back to the driver to check the chronology and separates agreement about the wording from verification of a medical finding, then attaches the identified clinical material; any decision about further investigation or work allocation remains for the reviewing professional, and the note itself does not certify that all relevant clinical questions have been answered.

If there is no clinical indication of a visual field 
impairment or a progressive eye condition, 
then it is satisfactory to screen for defect by 
confrontation. Confrontation is an inexact test. 
Any person who has, or is suspected of having, 
a visual field defect should have a formal 
perimetry-based assessment. 
Monocular automated static perimetry is the 
minimum baseline standard for visual field 
assessments. If monocular automated static 
perimetry shows no visual field defect, this 
information is sufficient to confirm that the 
standard is met. 
Subjects with any significant field defect or a 
progressive eye condition require a binocular 
Esterman visual field for assessment. This is 
classically done on a Humphrey visual field 
analyser, but any machine that can be shown 
to be equivalent is accepted (e.g. Medmont 
binocular VF printed off in level map mode). 
The treating optometrist or ophthalmologist 
can determine whether it is appropriate for the 
person to wear their normal corrective lenses 
while undergoing testing. Fixation monitoring 
must be performed and recorded on the test. 
Alternative devices must have the ability to 
monitor fixation and to stimulate the same 
spots as the standard binocular Esterman. For 
an Esterman binocular chart to be considered 
reliable for licensing, the false-positive score 
must be no more than 20 per cent."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-117af1818c65d4ad", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-117af1818c65d4ad | Commercial standards with qualifications", "node_id": "0053", "section": "10.3", "pdf_page": 221, "original_text": "Commercial standards

For the purposes of this publication, visual 
fields are defined as a measure of the extent 
of peripheral (side) vision. Normal visual field is: 
60 degrees nasally, 100 degrees temporally, 75 
degrees inferiorly and 60 degrees superiorly. 
The binocular field extends the horizontal extent 
from 160 to 200 degrees, with the central 120 
degrees overlapping and providing the potential 
for stereopsis. 
Visual fields may be reduced due to a range 
of neurological conditions (e.g. stroke, multiple 
sclerosis) as well by ocular diseases (e.g. 
glaucoma), or injuries, resulting in hemionopia, 
quadrantanopia or monocularity. 
Peripheral vision assists the driver to be aware 
of the total driving environment. Once alerted, 
the central fovea area is moved to identify 
the importance of the information. Therefore, 
peripheral vision loss that is incomplete will 
still allow awareness; this includes small areas 
of loss and patchy loss. Additionally, affected 
drivers can adapt to the defect by scanning 
regularly and effectively and can have good 
awareness. Patients with visual field defects 
who have full intellectual/cognitive capacity 
are more able to adapt, but those with such 
impairments will have decreased awareness and 
are therefore not safe to drive.
A longstanding field defect, such as from 
childhood, may lead to visual adaptation. Such 
defects need to be assessed by an optometrist 
or ophthalmologist for a conditional licence 
to be considered. They should be managed 
as an exceptional case to the standard, with 
consideration for duration and evidence of visual 
adaptation, whether the location of the defect is 
an area that may already be blocked by the car 
door on the passenger side (i.e. the inferior field 
on the left side without central field loss), driver 
safety record and the nature of the driving task."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-e8267bf4145306c0", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-e8267bf4145306c0 | 10.2.6. Colour vision", "node_id": "0039", "section": "10.2.6", "pdf_page": 218, "original_text": "10.2.6. Colour vision

normal road rules and conditions. A standard

A current signed perimetry assessment confirms a visual field defect and reports a binocular horizontal extent of 130 degrees, although the driver can still read central letters clearly and points to an earlier normal acuity result; the report does not establish the required vertical test extent, stability of the field loss or whether other significant defects affect driving, and the specialist's detailed functional opinion remains pending.

Part of the usual route requires reversing near workers and reading changing signs before entering a customer site, although today's assessment takes place in a quiet room; the driver is asked to describe the sequence and timing of difficulties, and the note preserves the difference between an occupational concern, a suspected mechanism and a completed clinical assessment.

Before closing the interview, the nurse checks that the driver's recollection and the supplied clinical document have not been merged into a single undated finding, and records the outstanding documents separately; the completed entries remain current findings, while any missing qualification, conflicting detail or unperformed examination stays available for review rather than being silently treated as normal.

If there is no clinical indication of a visual field 
impairment or a progressive eye condition, 
then it is satisfactory to screen for defect by

Any person who has, or is suspected of having, 
a visual field defect should have a formal 
perimetry-based assessment. 
Monocular automated static perimetry is the 
minimum baseline standard for visual field 
assessments. If monocular automated static 
perimetry shows no visual field defect, this 
information is sufficient to confirm that the 
standard is met. 
Subjects with any significant field defect or a 
progressive eye condition require a binocular 
Esterman visual field for assessment. This is 
classically done on a Humphrey visual field 
analyser, but any machine that can be shown 
to be equivalent is accepted (e.g. Medmont 
binocular VF printed off in level map mode). 
The treating optometrist or ophthalmologist 
can determine whether it is appropriate for the 
person to wear their normal corrective lenses 
while undergoing testing. Fixation monitoring 
must be performed and recorded on the test. 
Alternative devices must have the ability to 
monitor fixation and to stimulate the same 
spots as the standard binocular Esterman. For 
an Esterman binocular chart to be considered 
reliable for licensing, the false-positive score 
must be no more than 20 per cent."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-a5934e81e0aee450", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-a5934e81e0aee450 | • any central loss that is an extension of a hemianopia or quadrantanopia of size greater than three missed points.", "node_id": "0027", "section": "10.2.2", "pdf_page": 216, "original_text": "•

For the purposes of this publication, visual 
fields are defined as a measure of the extent 
of peripheral (side) vision. Normal visual field is: 
60 degrees nasally, 100 degrees temporally, 75 
degrees inferiorly and 60 degrees superiorly. 
The binocular field extends the horizontal extent 
from 160 to 200 degrees, with the central 120 
degrees overlapping and providing the potential 
for stereopsis. 
Visual fields may be reduced due to a range 
of neurological conditions (e.g. stroke, multiple 
sclerosis) as well by ocular diseases (e.g. 
glaucoma), or injuries, resulting in hemionopia, 
quadrantanopia or monocularity. 
Peripheral vision assists the driver to be aware 
of the total driving environment. Once alerted, 
the central fovea area is moved to identify 
the importance of the information. Therefore, 
peripheral vision loss that is incomplete will 
still allow awareness; this includes small areas 
of loss and patchy loss. Additionally, affected 
drivers can adapt to the defect by scanning 
regularly and effectively and can have good 
awareness. Patients with visual field defects 
who have full intellectual/cognitive capacity 
are more able to adapt, but those with such 
impairments will have decreased awareness and 
are therefore not safe to drive.
A longstanding field defect, such as from 
childhood, may lead to visual adaptation. Such 
defects need to be assessed by an optometrist 
or ophthalmologist for a conditional licence 
to be considered. They should be managed 
as an exceptional case to the standard, with 
consideration for duration and evidence of visual 
adaptation, whether the location of the defect is 
an area that may already be blocked by the car 
door on the passenger side (i.e. the inferior field 
on the left side without central field loss), driver 
safety record and the nature of the driving task."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-117af1818c65d4ad", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-117af1818c65d4ad | Commercial standards with qualifications", "node_id": "0053", "section": "10.3", "pdf_page": 221, "original_text": "Commercial standards

The evidence is incomplete regarding visual 
fields and visual acuity and crash risk. This is 
likely due to the many methodological reasons 
outlined in Part A of this publication (refer to Part 
A section 1.5. Development and evidence base). 
Identifying the degree to which reduced visual 
acuity increases motor vehicle crash risk is 
challenging. The evidence for visual acuity 
impairment is generally limited to drivers whose 
visual acuity already meets licensing standards, 
limiting the ability to determine whether 
alternative cut-points are more appropriate. 
While it is generally agreed that adequate visual 
fields are important for safe driving, the actual 
cut-off value that should be set remains unclear.
Most research suggests there is no association 
between crash risk and colour vision. While 
there is evidence that people with red-colour-
deficient vision have difficulty in detecting 
red lights and stopping in laboratory and on-
road testing, significant improvements in road 
engineering mean that people with red-colour 
deficiency may largely compensate for their 
deficiency while driving."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-VIS-COM-006", "title": "AFTD2022-VIS-COM-006 | Monocular vision", "node_id": "0056", "section": "10.3", "pdf_page": 221, "original_text": "A person is not fit to hold an unconditional

If there is no clinical indication of a visual field 
impairment or a progressive eye condition, 
then it is satisfactory to screen for defect by 
confrontation. Confrontation is an inexact test. 
Any person who has, or is suspected of having, 
a visual field defect should have a formal 
perimetry-based assessment. 
Monocular automated static perimetry is the 
minimum baseline standard for visual field 
assessments. If monocular automated static 
perimetry shows no visual field defect, this 
information is sufficient to confirm that the 
standard is met. 
Subjects with any significant field defect or a 
progressive eye condition require a binocular 
Esterman visual field for assessment. This is 
classically done on a Humphrey visual field 
analyser, but any machine that can be shown 
to be equivalent is accepted (e.g. Medmont 
binocular VF printed off in level map mode). 
The treating optometrist or ophthalmologist 
can determine whether it is appropriate for the 
person to wear their normal corrective lenses 
while undergoing testing. Fixation monitoring 
must be performed and recorded on the test. 
Alternative devices must have the ability to 
monitor fixation and to stimulate the same 
spots as the standard binocular Esterman. For 
an Esterman binocular chart to be considered 
reliable for licensing, the false-positive score 
must be no more than 20 per cent."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-a5934e81e0aee450", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-a5934e81e0aee450 | • any central loss that is an extension of a hemianopia or quadrantanopia of size greater than three missed points.", "node_id": "0027", "section": "10.2.2", "pdf_page": 216, "original_text": "•

The evidence is incomplete regarding visual 
fields and visual acuity and crash risk. This is 
likely due to the many methodological reasons 
outlined in Part A of this publication (refer to Part 
A section 1.5. Development and evidence base). 
Identifying the degree to which reduced visual 
acuity increases motor vehicle crash risk is 
challenging. The evidence for visual acuity 
impairment is generally limited to drivers whose 
visual acuity already meets licensing standards, 
limiting the ability to determine whether 
alternative cut-points are more appropriate. 
While it is generally agreed that adequate visual 
fields are important for safe driving, the actual 
cut-off value that should be set remains unclear.
Most research suggests there is no association 
between crash risk and colour vision. While 
there is evidence that people with red-colour-
deficient vision have difficulty in detecting 
red lights and stopping in laboratory and on-
road testing, significant improvements in road 
engineering mean that people with red-colour 
deficiency may largely compensate for their 
deficiency while driving."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-adb72bb1f206f023", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-adb72bb1f206f023 | 10.2.2. Visual fields3–6,8–13", "node_id": "0025", "section": "10.2.2", "pdf_page": 215, "original_text": "10.2.2. Visual fields3–6,8–13
For the purposes of this publication, visual 
fields are defined as a measure of the extent 
of peripheral (side) vision. Normal visual field is: 
60 degrees nasally, 100 degrees temporally, 75 
degrees inferiorly and 60 degrees superiorly. 
The binocular field extends the horizontal extent 
from 160 to 200 degrees, with the central 120 
degrees overlapping and providing the potential 
for stereopsis. 
Visual fields may be reduced due to a range 
of neurological conditions (e.g. stroke, multiple 
sclerosis) as well by ocular diseases (e.g. 
glaucoma), or injuries, resulting in hemionopia, 
quadrantanopia or monocularity. 
Peripheral vision assists the driver to be aware 
of the total driving environment. Once alerted, 
the central fovea area is moved to identify 
the importance of the information. Therefore, 
peripheral vision loss that is incomplete will 
still allow awareness; this includes small areas 
of loss and patchy loss. Additionally, affected 
drivers can adapt to the defect by scanning 
regularly and effectively and can have good 
awareness. Patients with visual field defects 
who have full intellectual/cognitive capacity 
are more able to adapt, but those with such 
impairments will have decreased awareness and 
are therefore not safe to drive.
A longstanding field defect, such as from 
childhood, may lead to visual adaptation. Such 
defects need to be assessed by an optometrist 
or ophthalmologist for a conditional licence 
to be considered. They should be managed 
as an exceptional case to the standard, with 
consideration for duration and evidence of visual 
adaptation, whether the location of the defect is 
an area that may already be blocked by the car 
door on the passenger side (i.e. the inferior field 
on the left side without central field loss), driver 
safety record and the nature of the driving task."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-a09b64ac70a92828", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-a09b64ac70a92828 | Commercial standards with qualifications", "node_id": "0049", "section": "10.3", "pdf_page": 220, "original_text": "Commercial standards

A conditional licence may be considered

If the person’s vision is worse than 6/18 in

The nurse reviews a commercial driver's symptoms alongside information from a witness, the treating team and an older workplace form, because each source describes a different part of the story; the occupational record retains those differences and identifies completed current findings without turning a booking, a family account or a recollection into a measured patient result.

The optometrist's current signed sheet records uncorrected visual acuity of 6/12 in the right eye and 6/18 in the left eye, then records corrected visual acuity of 6/6 in the right eye and 6/9 in the left eye with the prescribed lenses; the same specialist assessment documents no visual field defect, no diplopia and binocular rather than monocular vision, while the driver's recollection of driving comfortably without spectacles is retained as an account of behaviour rather than an alternative measurement.

The usual work involves coupling trailers, checking mirrors, interpreting radio messages and responding to pedestrians in a loading area, with breaks that can be delayed when deliveries run late; the driver explains which difficulty occurred while stationary and which was noticed during ordinary duties, rather than claiming that quiet conversation in the clinic reproduces every task in the cab.

The same current clinical review separately confirms that the driver has diabetes and is acutely unwell with metabolically unstable diabetes after vomiting and urgent glucose assessment; an older well-visit result is present in the folder, but the current physician has not documented resolution of this separate acute condition.

For the occupational reviewer, the nurse retains both the definite findings and the limitations of the available account, including the timing and testing conditions where they matter, rather than producing a single reassuring label; the driver is told which information is on file and which details still require confirmation, without replacing the recorded clinical evidence with an employer's preference.

The optometrist's current signed sheet records uncorrected visual acuity of 6/12 in the right eye and 6/18 in the left eye, then records corrected visual acuity of 6/6 in the right eye and 6/9 in the left eye with the prescribed lenses; the same specialist assessment documents no visual field defect, no diplopia and binocular rather than monocular vision, while the driver's recollection of driving comfortably without spectacles is retained as an account of behaviour rather than an alternative measurement.

The usual work involves coupling trailers, checking mirrors, interpreting radio messages and responding to pedestrians in a loading area, with breaks that can be delayed when deliveries run late; the driver explains which difficulty occurred while stationary and which was noticed during ordinary duties, rather than claiming that quiet conversation in the clinic reproduces every task in the cab.

The same current clinical review separately confirms that the driver has diabetes and is acutely unwell with metabolically unstable diabetes after vomiting and urgent glucose assessment; an older well-visit result is present in the folder, but the current physician has not documented resolution of this separate acute condition.

For the occupational reviewer, the nurse retains both the definite findings and the limitations of the available account, including the timing and testing conditions where they matter, rather than producing a single reassuring label; the driver is told which information is on file and which details still require confirmation, without replacing the recorded clinical evidence with an employer's preference.

If a severe hypoglycaemic event occurs (as 
defined in section 3.2.1. Hypoglycaemia), the 
person should not drive for a significant period 
of time and will need to be urgently assessed. 
The minimum period of time before returning 
to drive is generally six weeks because it often 
takes many weeks for patterns of glucose 
control and behaviour to be re-established and 
for any temporary ‘impaired hypoglycaemia 
awareness’ to resolve (see below). The non-
driving period will depend on factors such 
as identifying the reason for the episode, the 
specialist’s opinion and the type of motor vehicle 
licence. The specialist’s recommendation for 
returning to driving should be based on the 
patient’s behaviour and objective measures of 
glycaemic control (documented blood glucose) 
over a reasonable interval. 
Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness 10–14
Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness exists when 
a person does not regularly sense the usual 
early warning symptoms of mild hypoglycaemia 
such as sweating, tremulousness, hunger, 
tingling around the mouth, palpitations and 
headache. It markedly increases the risk of a 
severe hypoglycaemic event occurring and is 
therefore a risk for road safety. Rates of severe 
hypoglycaemia may be up to seven times higher 
compared with those who retain hypoglycaemia 
awareness. Impaired hypoglycaemia awareness 
occurs in 20–25 per cent of people with type 
1 diabetes and about 10 per cent of those with 
type 2 diabetes. Prevalence is higher in older 
people and in those with a longer duration 
of diabetes."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-0f4bda9270b6616d", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-0f4bda9270b6616d | brain function and may cause impairment of perception, motor skills or consciousness. While driving ability per se might not be affected 
by a hearing loss, responsiveness to critical 
events is an important safety consideration for 
drivers of commercial vehicles. These drivers 
therefore require the capacity to ensure safety 
and the capacity to respond to environmental 
situations that may involve sirens, rail crossings 
and emergency signals as well as conditions 
of the vehicle and roads. It may be challenging 
to rely solely on vision to compensate for a 
significant hearing loss in a commercial vehicle. 
The internal commercial vehicle cabin can 
place additional attentional, workload and visual 
demands on drivers for undertaking tasks such 
as checking multiple displays or monitors and 
using communication systems. These additional 
tasks reduce capacity to compensate for a lack 
of hearing by relying on vision to monitor the 
external environment."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-cc5b5152249058a5", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-cc5b5152249058a5 | 4.1.1. Effect of hearing loss on driving1–7", "node_id": "0007", "section": "4.1.1", "pdf_page": 116, "original_text": "4.1.1. Effect of hearing loss on 
driving1–7
The evidence base regarding hearing loss and 
driving safely is limited; however, the analysis 
of the small number of quality studies report 
that hearing loss has no effect on motor vehicle 
crash risk.1 It may be that a loss of hearing is 
well compensated for since most people who 
are hard of hearing are aware of their disability 
and therefore tend to be more cautious and rely 
more on visual cues and other sensations such 
as vibrations. Functional hearing is used in the 
driving task to:
•	
sense alarms, notifications and other 
auditory cues in the driving environment (e.g. 
railway crossings, first responder sirens) 
•	
sense auditory cues on the state and 
position of the vehicle from vehicle 
technology systems (e.g. alarms, warning 
systems using sound alerts)"}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-1ca53671ba0f3fb4", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-1ca53671ba0f3fb4 | Licensing responsibility The responsibility for issuing, renewing, suspending or cancelling a person’s driver licence (including a conditional licence) lies ultimately with the driver licensing authority.", "node_id": "0018", "section": "4.2.2", "pdf_page": 121, "original_text": "Licensing responsibility

While driving ability per se might not be affected 
by a hearing loss, responsiveness to critical 
events is an important safety consideration for 
drivers of commercial vehicles. These drivers 
therefore require the capacity to ensure safety 
and the capacity to respond to environmental 
situations that may involve sirens, rail crossings 
and emergency signals as well as conditions 
of the vehicle and roads. It may be challenging 
to rely solely on vision to compensate for a 
significant hearing loss in a commercial vehicle. 
The internal commercial vehicle cabin can 
place additional attentional, workload and visual 
demands on drivers for undertaking tasks such 
as checking multiple displays or monitors and 
using communication systems. These additional 
tasks reduce capacity to compensate for a lack 
of hearing by relying on vision to monitor the 
external environment."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-ac9c0c76b5ead534", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-ac9c0c76b5ead534 | Refer also to Part B section 5. Musculoskeletal conditions and section 10. If there is no clinical indication of a visual field 
impairment or a progressive eye condition, 
then it is satisfactory to screen for defect by 
confrontation. Confrontation is an inexact test. 
Any person who has, or is suspected of having, 
a visual field defect should have a formal 
perimetry-based assessment. 
Monocular automated static perimetry is the 
minimum baseline standard for visual field 
assessments. If monocular automated static 
perimetry shows no visual field defect, this 
information is sufficient to confirm that the 
standard is met. 
Subjects with any significant field defect or a 
progressive eye condition require a binocular 
Esterman visual field for assessment. This is 
classically done on a Humphrey visual field 
analyser, but any machine that can be shown 
to be equivalent is accepted (e.g. Medmont 
binocular VF printed off in level map mode). 
The treating optometrist or ophthalmologist 
can determine whether it is appropriate for the 
person to wear their normal corrective lenses 
while undergoing testing. Fixation monitoring 
must be performed and recorded on the test. 
Alternative devices must have the ability to 
monitor fixation and to stimulate the same 
spots as the standard binocular Esterman. For 
an Esterman binocular chart to be considered 
reliable for licensing, the false-positive score 
must be no more than 20 per cent."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-a5934e81e0aee450", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-a5934e81e0aee450 | • any central loss that is an extension of a hemianopia or quadrantanopia of size greater than three missed points.", "node_id": "0027", "section": "10.2.2", "pdf_page": 216, "original_text": "•

For the purposes of this publication, visual 
fields are defined as a measure of the extent 
of peripheral (side) vision. Normal visual field is: 
60 degrees nasally, 100 degrees temporally, 75 
degrees inferiorly and 60 degrees superiorly. 
The binocular field extends the horizontal extent 
from 160 to 200 degrees, with the central 120 
degrees overlapping and providing the potential 
for stereopsis. 
Visual fields may be reduced due to a range 
of neurological conditions (e.g. stroke, multiple 
sclerosis) as well by ocular diseases (e.g. 
glaucoma), or injuries, resulting in hemionopia, 
quadrantanopia or monocularity. 
Peripheral vision assists the driver to be aware 
of the total driving environment. Once alerted, 
the central fovea area is moved to identify 
the importance of the information. Therefore, 
peripheral vision loss that is incomplete will 
still allow awareness; this includes small areas 
of loss and patchy loss. Additionally, affected 
drivers can adapt to the defect by scanning 
regularly and effectively and can have good 
awareness. Patients with visual field defects 
who have full intellectual/cognitive capacity 
are more able to adapt, but those with such 
impairments will have decreased awareness and 
are therefore not safe to drive.
A longstanding field defect, such as from 
childhood, may lead to visual adaptation. Such 
defects need to be assessed by an optometrist 
or ophthalmologist for a conditional licence 
to be considered. They should be managed 
as an exceptional case to the standard, with 
consideration for duration and evidence of visual 
adaptation, whether the location of the defect is 
an area that may already be blocked by the car 
door on the passenger side (i.e. the inferior field 
on the left side without central field loss), driver 
safety record and the nature of the driving task."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-b9f8c41dbdf5f5ac", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-b9f8c41dbdf5f5ac | The nature of the driving task The driver licensing authority will take into consideration the nature of the driving task as well as the medical condition, particularly when granting a conditional licence. The evidence is incomplete regarding visual 
fields and visual acuity and crash risk. This is 
likely due to the many methodological reasons 
outlined in Part A of this publication (refer to Part 
A section 1.5. Development and evidence base). 
Identifying the degree to which reduced visual 
acuity increases motor vehicle crash risk is 
challenging. The evidence for visual acuity 
impairment is generally limited to drivers whose 
visual acuity already meets licensing standards, 
limiting the ability to determine whether 
alternative cut-points are more appropriate. 
While it is generally agreed that adequate visual 
fields are important for safe driving, the actual 
cut-off value that should be set remains unclear.
Most research suggests there is no association 
between crash risk and colour vision. While 
there is evidence that people with red-colour-
deficient vision have difficulty in detecting 
red lights and stopping in laboratory and on-
road testing, significant improvements in road 
engineering mean that people with red-colour 
deficiency may largely compensate for their

The commercial driver attends after a long shift with a folder containing a current signed letter, older screening paperwork and a handwritten personal account, and the nurse reconstructs the chronology before recording the present findings; differences between the records are described explicitly rather than resolved by treating the newest-looking photocopy as automatically authoritative.

A current signed perimetry assessment confirms a visual field defect and reports a binocular horizontal extent of 135 degrees, although the driver can still read central letters clearly and points to an earlier normal acuity result; the report does not establish the required vertical test extent, stability of the field loss or whether other significant defects affect driving, and the specialist's detailed functional opinion remains pending.

The interview takes place before the driver's next planned roster, and the nurse records changes in symptoms, treatment and available documents without assuming that a future specialist appointment has already occurred; any letter that has been requested but not supplied remains separate from the findings actually available when this occupational record is written.

For the occupational reviewer, the nurse retains both the definite findings and the limitations of the available account, including the timing and testing conditions where they matter, rather than producing a single reassuring label; the driver is told which information is on file and which details still require confirmation, without replacing the recorded clinical evidence with an employer's preference.

For the purposes of this publication, visual 
fields are defined as a measure of the extent 
of peripheral (side) vision. Normal visual field is: 
60 degrees nasally, 100 degrees temporally, 75 
degrees inferiorly and 60 degrees superiorly. 
The binocular field extends the horizontal extent 
from 160 to 200 degrees, with the central 120 
degrees overlapping and providing the potential 
for stereopsis. 
Visual fields may be reduced due to a range 
of neurological conditions (e.g. stroke, multiple 
sclerosis) as well by ocular diseases (e.g. 
glaucoma), or injuries, resulting in hemionopia, 
quadrantanopia or monocularity. 
Peripheral vision assists the driver to be aware 
of the total driving environment. Once alerted, 
the central fovea area is moved to identify 
the importance of the information. Therefore, 
peripheral vision loss that is incomplete will 
still allow awareness; this includes small areas 
of loss and patchy loss. Additionally, affected 
drivers can adapt to the defect by scanning 
regularly and effectively and can have good 
awareness. Patients with visual field defects 
who have full intellectual/cognitive capacity 
are more able to adapt, but those with such 
impairments will have decreased awareness and 
are therefore not safe to drive.
A longstanding field defect, such as from 
childhood, may lead to visual adaptation. Such 
defects need to be assessed by an optometrist 
or ophthalmologist for a conditional licence 
to be considered. They should be managed 
as an exceptional case to the standard, with 
consideration for duration and evidence of visual 
adaptation, whether the location of the defect is 
an area that may already be blocked by the car 
door on the passenger side (i.e. the inferior field 
on the left side without central field loss), driver 
safety record and the nature of the driving task."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-072f14c5d1083124", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-072f14c5d1083124 | Assessment method", "node_id": "0024", "section": "10.2.2", "pdf_page": 215, "original_text": "Assessment method
If there is no clinical indication of a visual field 
impairment or a progressive eye condition, 
then it is satisfactory to screen for defect by 
confrontation. Confrontation is an inexact test. 
Any person who has, or is suspected of having, 
a visual field defect should have a formal 
perimetry-based assessment. 
Monocular automated static perimetry is the 
minimum baseline standard for visual field 
assessments. If monocular automated static 
perimetry shows no visual field defect, this 
information is sufficient to confirm that the 
standard is met. 
Subjects with any significant field defect or a 
progressive eye condition require a binocular 
Esterman visual field for assessment. This is 
classically done on a Humphrey visual field 
analyser, but any machine that can be shown 
to be equivalent is accepted (e.g. Medmont 
binocular VF printed off in level map mode). 
The treating optometrist or ophthalmologist 
can determine whether it is appropriate for the 
person to wear their normal corrective lenses 
while undergoing testing. Fixation monitoring 
must be performed and recorded on the test. 
Alternative devices must have the ability to 
monitor fixation and to stimulate the same 
spots as the standard binocular Esterman. For 
an Esterman binocular chart to be considered 
reliable for licensing, the false-positive score 
must be no more than 20 per cent."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-117af1818c65d4ad", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-117af1818c65d4ad | Commercial standards with qualifications", "node_id": "0053", "section": "10.3", "pdf_page": 221, "original_text": "Commercial standards

Decline in vision is associated with normal 
ageing and is therefore an important 
consideration for fitness to drive in the general 
care of older people, along with consideration 
of cognition and sensory-motor function (refer 
to Part A section 2.2.7. Older drivers and age-
related changes). 
Progressive eye conditions such as cataracts, 
glaucoma and macular degeneration are also 
more common in older people. Once diagnosed, 
these conditions require regular monitoring in 
relation to driving, including through conditional 
licences as appropriate (refer to section 
10.2.4. Progressive eye conditions). Regular 
monitoring is also required for conditions such 
as diabetes to screen for and manage end-
organ effects (retinopathy) (refer to section 3.2.3. 
Comorbidities and end-organ complications).
For drivers with neurological conditions such as 
stroke, vision is one of a number of functional 
outcomes that will be addressed as part of 
an overall assessment of fitness to drive, and 
findings will need to be integrated as part of 
this overall assessment (refer to section 6.3.

conditions)."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-0fe8bf8cdf4b51c6", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-0fe8bf8cdf4b51c6 | 10.2.3. Diplopia", "node_id": "0030", "section": "10.2.3", "pdf_page": 217, "original_text": "10.2.3. Diplopia

{"module": "diabetes", "licence_context": "commercial", "query": "Synthetic nurse note for software testing. No real patient data.

The nurse reviews a commercial driver's symptoms alongside information from a witness, the treating team and an older workplace form, because each source describes a different part of the story; the occupational record retains those differences and identifies completed current findings without turning a booking, a family account or a recollection into a measured patient result.

The specialist's current referral identifies gestational diabetes during pregnancy and confirms that insulin has recently been introduced, rather than documenting pre-existing chronic diabetes; the driver reports variable appetite on early starts but no confirmed severe hypoglycaemic event is described, and the nurse distinguishes the self-limiting pregnancy-related condition from chronic insulin-treated diabetes while requesting advice about current symptoms and short-term driving fitness.

The driver alternates urban deliveries with a longer motorway leg and describes a busy depot where engine noise, glare and interrupted meals can complicate an account of symptoms; the nurse records the work setting as context, while keeping the dated clinical findings distinct from the driver's explanation for why a symptom might have occurred on that shift.

Before closing the interview, the nurse checks that the driver's recollection and the supplied clinical document have not been merged into a single undated finding, and records the outstanding documents separately; the completed entries remain current findings, while any missing qualification, conflicting detail or unperformed examination stays available for review rather than being silently treated as normal.

licences for commercial vehicle drivers are 
issued by the driver licensing authority based on 
advice from an appropriate medical specialist 
(endocrinologist or consultant physician

are reviewed periodically by the specialist to

commercial drivers receiving insulin treatment, at

to drive."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-d6142190f29b7662", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-d6142190f29b7662 | Vision", "node_id": "0028", "section": "3.2.3", "pdf_page": 106, "original_text": "Vision

Visual acuity should be tested annually. Retinal 
screening should be undertaken every second 
year if there is no retinopathy, or more frequently 
if at high risk. Visual field testing is not required 
unless clinically indicated.7,8
Neuropathy and foot care
While it can be difficult to be prescriptive 
about neuropathy in the context of driving, it is 
important that the severity of the condition is 
assessed. Adequate sensation and movement 
for the operation of foot controls is required 
(refer to section 6. Neurological conditions and 
section 5. Musculoskeletal conditions).
Sleep apnoea
Sleep apnoea is a common comorbidity 
affecting many people with type 2 diabetes and 
has substantial implications for road safety. The 
treating health professional should be alert to 
potential signs (e.g. BMI greater than 35) and 
symptoms, and apply the Epworth Sleepiness 
Scale as appropriate (refer to section 8. Sleep 
disorders).

There are no diabetes-specific medical 
standards for cardiovascular risk factors and 
driver licensing. Consistent with good medical 
practice, people with diabetes should have their 
cardiovascular risk factors periodically assessed 
and treated as required (refer to section 2.

Potential causes7
Hypoglycaemia may be caused by many 
factors including non-adherence or alteration 
to medication, unexpected exertion, alcohol 
intake or irregular meals. Meal regularity and 
variability in medication administration may 
be important considerations for long-distance 
commercial driving or for drivers operating 
on shifts. Impairment of consciousness and 
judgement can develop rapidly and result in loss 
of control of a vehicle. Excessively tight control 
may contribute to hypoglycaemia.
Advice to drivers
The driver should be advised not to drive if a 
severe hypoglycaemic event is experienced 
while driving or at any other time, until they have 
been cleared to drive by a medical practitioner.

If a severe hypoglycaemic event occurs (as 
defined in section 3.2.1. Hypoglycaemia), the 
person should not drive for a significant period 
of time and will need to be urgently assessed. 
The minimum period of time before returning 
to drive is generally six weeks because it often 
takes many weeks for patterns of glucose 
control and behaviour to be re-established and 
for any temporary ‘impaired hypoglycaemia 
awareness’ to resolve (see below). The non-
driving period will depend on factors such 
as identifying the reason for the episode, the 
specialist’s opinion and the type of motor vehicle 
licence. The specialist’s recommendation for 
returning to driving should be based on the 
patient’s behaviour and objective measures of 
glycaemic control (documented blood glucose) 
over a reasonable interval. 
Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness 10–14
Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness exists when 
a person does not regularly sense the usual 
early warning symptoms of mild hypoglycaemia 
such as sweating, tremulousness, hunger, 
tingling around the mouth, palpitations and 
headache. It markedly increases the risk of a 
severe hypoglycaemic event occurring and is 
therefore a risk for road safety. Rates of severe 
hypoglycaemia may be up to seven times higher 
compared with those who retain hypoglycaemia 
awareness. Impaired hypoglycaemia awareness 
occurs in 20–25 per cent of people with type 
1 diabetes and about 10 per cent of those with 
type 2 diabetes. Prevalence is higher in older 
people and in those with a longer duration 
of diabetes."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-c699baaa6241423e", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-c699baaa6241423e | 3.1.2. Evidence of crash risk1,4–7", "node_id": "0010", "section": "3.1.2", "pdf_page": 103, "original_text": "3.1.2. Evidence of crash risk1,4–7

evidence that ‘tighter control’, as measured by 
the HbA1c, may be associated with increased

person should not drive for a significant period

takes many weeks for patterns of glucose

Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness exists when 
a person does not regularly sense the usual 
early warning symptoms of mild hypoglycaemia 
such as sweating, tremulousness, hunger, 
tingling around the mouth, palpitations and 
headache. It markedly increases the risk of a 
severe hypoglycaemic event occurring and is 
therefore a risk for road safety. Rates of severe 
hypoglycaemia may be up to seven times higher 
compared with those who retain hypoglycaemia 
awareness. Impaired hypoglycaemia awareness 
occurs in 20–25 per cent of people with type 
1 diabetes and about 10 per cent of those with 
type 2 diabetes. Prevalence is higher in older 
people and in those with a longer duration 
of diabetes."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-d6142190f29b7662", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-d6142190f29b7662 | Vision", "node_id": "0028", "section": "3.2.3", "pdf_page": 106, "original_text": "Vision

While driving ability per se might not be affected 
by a hearing loss, responsiveness to critical 
events is an important safety consideration for 
drivers of commercial vehicles. These drivers 
therefore require the capacity to ensure safety 
and the capacity to respond to environmental 
situations that may involve sirens, rail crossings 
and emergency signals as well as conditions 
of the vehicle and roads. It may be challenging 
to rely solely on vision to compensate for a 
significant hearing loss in a commercial vehicle. 
The internal commercial vehicle cabin can 
place additional attentional, workload and visual 
demands on drivers for undertaking tasks such 
as checking multiple displays or monitors and 
using communication systems. These additional 
tasks reduce capacity to compensate for a lack 
of hearing by relying on vision to monitor the 
external environment."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-cc5b5152249058a5", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-cc5b5152249058a5 | 4.1.1. Effect of hearing loss on driving1–7", "node_id": "0007", "section": "4.1.1", "pdf_page": 116, "original_text": "4.1.1. Effect of hearing loss on

{"module": "vision", "licence_context": "commercial", "query": "Synthetic nurse note for software testing. No real patient data.

The commercial driver attends after a long shift with a folder containing a current signed letter, older screening paperwork and a handwritten personal account, and the nurse reconstructs the chronology before recording the present findings; differences between the records are described explicitly rather than resolved by treating the newest-looking photocopy as automatically authoritative.

The optometrist's current signed sheet records uncorrected visual acuity of 6/12 in the right eye and 6/18 in the left eye, then records corrected visual acuity of 6/6 in the right eye and 6/9 in the left eye with the prescribed lenses; the same specialist assessment documents no visual field defect, no diplopia and binocular rather than monocular vision, while the driver's recollection of driving comfortably without spectacles is retained as an account of behaviour rather than an alternative measurement.

The driver alternates urban deliveries with a longer motorway leg and describes a busy depot where engine noise, glare and interrupted meals can complicate an account of symptoms; the nurse records the work setting as context, while keeping the dated clinical findings distinct from the driver's explanation for why a symptom might have occurred on that shift.

If there is no clinical indication of a visual field 
impairment or a progressive eye condition, 
then it is satisfactory to screen for defect by 
confrontation. Confrontation is an inexact test. 
Any person who has, or is suspected of having, 
a visual field defect should have a formal 
perimetry-based assessment. 
Monocular automated static perimetry is the 
minimum baseline standard for visual field 
assessments. If monocular automated static 
perimetry shows no visual field defect, this 
information is sufficient to confirm that the 
standard is met. 
Subjects with any significant field defect or a 
progressive eye condition require a binocular 
Esterman visual field for assessment. This is 
classically done on a Humphrey visual field 
analyser, but any machine that can be shown 
to be equivalent is accepted (e.g. Medmont 
binocular VF printed off in level map mode). 
The treating optometrist or ophthalmologist 
can determine whether it is appropriate for the 
person to wear their normal corrective lenses 
while undergoing testing. Fixation monitoring 
must be performed and recorded on the test. 
Alternative devices must have the ability to 
monitor fixation and to stimulate the same 
spots as the standard binocular Esterman. For 
an Esterman binocular chart to be considered 
reliable for licensing, the false-positive score 
must be no more than 20 per cent."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-adb72bb1f206f023", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-adb72bb1f206f023 | 10.2.2. Visual fields3–6,8–13", "node_id": "0025", "section": "10.2.2", "pdf_page": 215, "original_text": "10.2.2. Visual fields3–6,8–13
For the purposes of this publication, visual 
fields are defined as a measure of the extent 
of peripheral (side) vision. Normal visual field is: 
60 degrees nasally, 100 degrees temporally, 75 
degrees inferiorly and 60 degrees superiorly. 
The binocular field extends the horizontal extent 
from 160 to 200 degrees, with the central 120 
degrees overlapping and providing the potential 
for stereopsis. 
Visual fields may be reduced due to a range 
of neurological conditions (e.g. stroke, multiple 
sclerosis) as well by ocular diseases (e.g. 
glaucoma), or injuries, resulting in hemionopia, 
quadrantanopia or monocularity. 
Peripheral vision assists the driver to be aware 
of the total driving environment. Once alerted, 
the central fovea area is moved to identify 
the importance of the information. Therefore, 
peripheral vision loss that is incomplete will 
still allow awareness; this includes small areas 
of loss and patchy loss. Additionally, affected 
drivers can adapt to the defect by scanning 
regularly and effectively and can have good 
awareness. Patients with visual field defects 
who have full intellectual/cognitive capacity 
are more able to adapt, but those with such 
impairments will have decreased awareness and 
are therefore not safe to drive.
A longstanding field defect, such as from 
childhood, may lead to visual adaptation. Such 
defects need to be assessed by an optometrist 
or ophthalmologist for a conditional licence 
to be considered. They should be managed 
as an exceptional case to the standard, with 
consideration for duration and evidence of visual 
adaptation, whether the location of the defect is 
an area that may already be blocked by the car 
door on the passenger side (i.e. the inferior field 
on the left side without central field loss), driver 
safety record and the nature of the driving task."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-a09b64ac70a92828", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-a09b64ac70a92828 | Commercial standards with qualifications", "node_id": "0049", "section": "10.3", "pdf_page": 220, "original_text": "Commercial standards

The evidence is incomplete regarding visual 
fields and visual acuity and crash risk. This is 
likely due to the many methodological reasons 
outlined in Part A of this publication (refer to Part 
A section 1.5. Development and evidence base). 
Identifying the degree to which reduced visual 
acuity increases motor vehicle crash risk is 
challenging. The evidence for visual acuity 
impairment is generally limited to drivers whose 
visual acuity already meets licensing standards, 
limiting the ability to determine whether 
alternative cut-points are more appropriate. 
While it is generally agreed that adequate visual 
fields are important for safe driving, the actual 
cut-off value that should be set remains unclear.
Most research suggests there is no association 
between crash risk and colour vision. While 
there is evidence that people with red-colour-
deficient vision have difficulty in detecting 
red lights and stopping in laboratory and on-
road testing, significant improvements in road 
engineering mean that people with red-colour 
deficiency may largely compensate for their 
deficiency while driving."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-cd83e305301149c8", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-cd83e305301149c8 | 10.2.9. Practical driver assessments", "node_id": "0046", "section": "10.2.9", "pdf_page": 219, "original_text": "10.2.9. Practical driver assessments
A practical driver assessment is not considered 
to be a safe or reliable method of assessing 
the effects of disorders of vision on driving, 
especially the visual fields, because the driver’s 
response to emergency situations or various 
environmental conditions cannot be determined. 
Information about adaptation to visual field 
defects can be gained from visual field tests 
such as the Esterman.

If there is no clinical indication of a visual field 
impairment or a progressive eye condition, 
then it is satisfactory to screen for defect by 
confrontation. Confrontation is an inexact test. 
Any person who has, or is suspected of having, 
a visual field defect should have a formal 
perimetry-based assessment. 
Monocular automated static perimetry is the 
minimum baseline standard for visual field 
assessments. If monocular automated static 
perimetry shows no visual field defect, this 
information is sufficient to confirm that the 
standard is met. 
Subjects with any significant field defect or a 
progressive eye condition require a binocular 
Esterman visual field for assessment. This is 
classically done on a Humphrey visual field 
analyser, but any machine that can be shown 
to be equivalent is accepted (e.g. Medmont 
binocular VF printed off in level map mode). 
The treating optometrist or ophthalmologist 
can determine whether it is appropriate for the 
person to wear their normal corrective lenses 
while undergoing testing. Fixation monitoring 
must be performed and recorded on the test. 
Alternative devices must have the ability to 
monitor fixation and to stimulate the same 
spots as the standard binocular Esterman. For

For the purposes of this publication, visual 
fields are defined as a measure of the extent 
of peripheral (side) vision. Normal visual field is: 
60 degrees nasally, 100 degrees temporally, 75 
degrees inferiorly and 60 degrees superiorly. 
The binocular field extends the horizontal extent 
from 160 to 200 degrees, with the central 120 
degrees overlapping and providing the potential 
for stereopsis. 
Visual fields may be reduced due to a range 
of neurological conditions (e.g. stroke, multiple 
sclerosis) as well by ocular diseases (e.g. 
glaucoma), or injuries, resulting in hemionopia, 
quadrantanopia or monocularity. 
Peripheral vision assists the driver to be aware 
of the total driving environment. Once alerted, 
the central fovea area is moved to identify 
the importance of the information. Therefore, 
peripheral vision loss that is incomplete will 
still allow awareness; this includes small areas 
of loss and patchy loss. Additionally, affected 
drivers can adapt to the defect by scanning 
regularly and effectively and can have good 
awareness. Patients with visual field defects 
who have full intellectual/cognitive capacity 
are more able to adapt, but those with such 
impairments will have decreased awareness and 
are therefore not safe to drive.
A longstanding field defect, such as from 
childhood, may lead to visual adaptation. Such 
defects need to be assessed by an optometrist 
or ophthalmologist for a conditional licence 
to be considered. They should be managed 
as an exceptional case to the standard, with 
consideration for duration and evidence of visual 
adaptation, whether the location of the defect is 
an area that may already be blocked by the car 
door on the passenger side (i.e. the inferior field 
on the left side without central field loss), driver 
safety record and the nature of the driving task."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-cd83e305301149c8", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-cd83e305301149c8 | 10.2.9. Practical driver assessments", "node_id": "0046", "section": "10.2.9", "pdf_page": 219, "original_text": "10.2.9. Practical driver assessments

The evidence is incomplete regarding visual 
fields and visual acuity and crash risk. This is 
likely due to the many methodological reasons 
outlined in Part A of this publication (refer to Part 
A section 1.5. Development and evidence base). 
Identifying the degree to which reduced visual 
acuity increases motor vehicle crash risk is 
challenging. The evidence for visual acuity 
impairment is generally limited to drivers whose 
visual acuity already meets licensing standards, 
limiting the ability to determine whether 
alternative cut-points are more appropriate. 
While it is generally agreed that adequate visual 
fields are important for safe driving, the actual 
cut-off value that should be set remains unclear.
Most research suggests there is no association 
between crash risk and colour vision. While 
there is evidence that people with red-colour-
deficient vision have difficulty in detecting 
red lights and stopping in laboratory and on-
road testing, significant improvements in road 
engineering mean that people with red-colour 
deficiency may largely compensate for their 
deficiency while driving."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-db731186cdb786e3", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-db731186cdb786e3 | 10.2. General assessment and management guidelines", "node_id": "0012", "section": "10.2", "pdf_page": 213, "original_text": "10.2.	 General assessment

Decline in vision is associated with normal 
ageing and is therefore an important 
consideration for fitness to drive in the general 
care of older people, along with consideration 
of cognition and sensory-motor function (refer 
to Part A section 2.2.7. Older drivers and age-
related changes). 
Progressive eye conditions such as cataracts, 
glaucoma and macular degeneration are also 
more common in older people. Once diagnosed, 
these conditions require regular monitoring in 
relation to driving, including through conditional 
licences as appropriate (refer to section 
10.2.4. Progressive eye conditions). Regular 
monitoring is also required for conditions such 
as diabetes to screen for and manage end-

Comorbidities and end-organ complications).

stroke, vision is one of a number of functional

At a scheduled commercial-driver medical, the driver answers questions in several stages because a dispatcher keeps calling about the next route, while the nurse checks a current clinical document against a copied workplace summary; an observation described confidently in conversation is kept separate from a finding actually recorded in an identified examination.

The current ophthalmologist's signed examination confirms non-physiological diplopia within 19 degrees of central fixation, reproduced during the assessment even though the driver says the two overlapping road-sign images sometimes merge after blinking; an older note reported comfortable reading at a desk, but that earlier description neither contradicts the current reproduced double vision nor establishes that a patch or new lenses have resolved it.

The usual work involves coupling trailers, checking mirrors, interpreting radio messages and responding to pedestrians in a loading area, with breaks that can be delayed when deliveries run late; the driver explains which difficulty occurred while stationary and which was noticed during ordinary duties, rather than claiming that quiet conversation in the clinic reproduces every task in the cab.

The same current clinical review separately confirms that the driver has diabetes and is acutely unwell with metabolically unstable diabetes after vomiting and urgent glucose assessment; an older well-visit result is present in the folder, but the current physician has not documented resolution of this separate acute condition.

The record is prepared for the reviewing clinician with the sequence of events and the provenance of the available findings intact, because the employer summary and the driver's account answer different questions; a completed test is retained as such, but an unresolved detail is not filled in from a family member's history or from an earlier document with different testing conditions.

At a scheduled commercial-driver medical, the driver answers questions in several stages because a dispatcher keeps calling about the next route, while the nurse checks a current clinical document against a copied workplace summary; an observation described confidently in conversation is kept separate from a finding actually recorded in an identified examination.

The current ophthalmologist's signed examination confirms non-physiological diplopia within 19 degrees of central fixation, reproduced during the assessment even though the driver says the two overlapping road-sign images sometimes merge after blinking; an older note reported comfortable reading at a desk, but that earlier description neither contradicts the current reproduced double vision nor establishes that a patch or new lenses have resolved it.

The usual work involves coupling trailers, checking mirrors, interpreting radio messages and responding to pedestrians in a loading area, with breaks that can be delayed when deliveries run late; the driver explains which difficulty occurred while stationary and which was noticed during ordinary duties, rather than claiming that quiet conversation in the clinic reproduces every task in the cab.

The same current clinical review separately confirms that the driver has diabetes and is acutely unwell with metabolically unstable diabetes after vomiting and urgent glucose assessment; an older well-visit result is present in the folder, but the current physician has not documented resolution of this separate acute condition.

The record is prepared for the reviewing clinician with the sequence of events and the provenance of the available findings intact, because the employer summary and the driver's account answer different questions; a completed test is retained as such, but an unresolved detail is not filled in from a family member's history or from an earlier document with different testing conditions.

If a severe hypoglycaemic event occurs (as 
defined in section 3.2.1. Hypoglycaemia), the 
person should not drive for a significant period 
of time and will need to be urgently assessed. 
The minimum period of time before returning 
to drive is generally six weeks because it often 
takes many weeks for patterns of glucose 
control and behaviour to be re-established and 
for any temporary ‘impaired hypoglycaemia 
awareness’ to resolve (see below). The non-
driving period will depend on factors such 
as identifying the reason for the episode, the 
specialist’s opinion and the type of motor vehicle 
licence. The specialist’s recommendation for 
returning to driving should be based on the 
patient’s behaviour and objective measures of 
glycaemic control (documented blood glucose) 
over a reasonable interval. 
Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness 10–14
Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness exists when 
a person does not regularly sense the usual 
early warning symptoms of mild hypoglycaemia 
such as sweating, tremulousness, hunger, 
tingling around the mouth, palpitations and 
headache. It markedly increases the risk of a 
severe hypoglycaemic event occurring and is 
therefore a risk for road safety. Rates of severe 
hypoglycaemia may be up to seven times higher 
compared with those who retain hypoglycaemia 
awareness. Impaired hypoglycaemia awareness 
occurs in 20–25 per cent of people with type 
1 diabetes and about 10 per cent of those with 
type 2 diabetes. Prevalence is higher in older 
people and in those with a longer duration 
of diabetes."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-457570d561f8a4dd", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-457570d561f8a4dd | Patient Survey", "node_id": "0033", "section": "3.2.4", "pdf_page": 108, "original_text": "Patient Survey

{"module": "hearing", "licence_context": "commercial", "query": "Synthetic nurse note for software testing. No real patient data.

At a scheduled commercial-driver medical, the driver answers questions in several stages because a dispatcher keeps calling about the next route, while the nurse checks a current clinical document against a copied workplace summary; an observation described confidently in conversation is kept separate from a finding actually recorded in an identified examination.

The available test sheet reports a hearing average of 32 dB while both hearing aids were worn, but it does not supply an unaided better-ear result or a complete frequency list; the driver is able to follow a quiet face-to-face exchange yet repeatedly misses radio instructions beside an idling engine, and the nurse documents possible hearing loss without treating the aided number as an unaided threshold or assuming that all commercial assessment requirements were tested.

Part of the usual route requires reversing near workers and reading changing signs before entering a customer site, although today's assessment takes place in a quiet room; the driver is asked to describe the sequence and timing of difficulties, and the note preserves the difference between an occupational concern, a suspected mechanism and a completed clinical assessment.

The record is prepared for the reviewing clinician with the sequence of events and the provenance of the available findings intact, because the employer summary and the driver's account answer different questions; a completed test is retained as such, but an unresolved detail is not filled in from a family member's history or from an earlier document with different testing conditions.

While driving ability per se might not be affected 
by a hearing loss, responsiveness to critical 
events is an important safety consideration for 
drivers of commercial vehicles. These drivers 
therefore require the capacity to ensure safety 
and the capacity to respond to environmental 
situations that may involve sirens, rail crossings 
and emergency signals as well as conditions 
of the vehicle and roads. It may be challenging 
to rely solely on vision to compensate for a 
significant hearing loss in a commercial vehicle. 
The internal commercial vehicle cabin can 
place additional attentional, workload and visual 
demands on drivers for undertaking tasks such 
as checking multiple displays or monitors and 
using communication systems. These additional 
tasks reduce capacity to compensate for a lack 
of hearing by relying on vision to monitor the 
external environment."}, {"source_id": "AFTD2022-EXP-cc5b5152249058a5", "title": "AFTD2022-EXP-cc5b5152249058a5 | 4.1.1. Effect of hearing loss on driving1–7", "node_id": "0007", "section": "4.1.1", "pdf_page": 116, "original_text": "4.1.1. Effect of hearing loss on

{"module": "vision", "licence_context": "commercial", "query": "Synthetic nurse note for software testing. No real patient data.

The nurse reviews a commercial driver's symptoms alongside information from a witness, the treating team and an older workplace form, because each source describes a different part of the story; the occupational record retains those differences and identifies completed current findings without turning a booking, a family account or a recollection into a measured patient result.

A current signed perimetry assessment confirms a visual field defect and reports a binocular horizontal extent of 132 degrees, although the driver can still read central letters clearly and points to an earlier normal acuity result; the report does not establish the required vertical test extent, stability of the field loss or whether other significant defects affect driving, and the specialist's detailed functional opinion remains pending.

Part of the usual route requires reversing near workers and reading changing signs before entering a customer site, although today's assessment takes place in a quiet room; the driver is asked to describe the sequence and timing of difficulties, and the note preserves the difference between an occupational concern, a suspected mechanism and a completed clinical assessment.

The nurse reads the summary back to the driver to check the chronology and separates agreement about the wording from verification of a medical finding, then attaches the identified clinical material; any decision about further investigation or work allocation remains for the reviewing professional, and the note itself does not certify that all relevant clinical questions have been answered.

{"module": "vision", "licence_context": "commercial", "query": "Synthetic nurse note for software testing. No real patient data.

The nurse reviews a commercial driver's symptoms alongside information from a witness, the treating team and an older workplace form, because each source describes a different part of the story; the occupational record retains those differences and identifies completed current findings without turning a booking, a family account or a recollection into a measured patient result.

A current signed perimetry assessment confirms a visual field defect and reports a binocular horizontal extent of 132 degrees, although the driver can still read central letters clearly and points to an earlier normal acuity result; the report does not establish the required vertical test extent, stability of the field loss or whether other significant defects affect driving, and the specialist's detailed functional opinion remains pending.

Part of the usual route requires reversing near workers and reading changing signs before entering a customer site, although today's assessment takes place in a quiet room; the driver is asked to describe the sequence and timing of difficulties, and the note preserves the difference between an occupational concern, a suspected mechanism and a completed clinical assessment.

The nurse reads the summary back to the driver to check the chronology and separates agreement about the wording from verification of a medical finding, then attaches the identified clinical material; any decision about further investigation or work allocation remains for the reviewing professional, and the note itself does not certify that all relevant clinical questions have been answered.

If there is no clinical indication of a visual field 
impairment or a progressive eye condition, 
then it is satisfactory to screen for defect by 
confrontation. Confrontation is an inexact test. 
Any person who has, or is suspected of having, 
a visual field defect should have a formal 
perimetry-based assessment. 
Monocular automated static perimetry is the 
minimum baseline standard for visual field 
assessments. If monocular automated static 
perimetry shows no visual field defect, this 
information is sufficient to confirm that the 
standard is met. 
Subjects with any significant field defect or a 
progressive eye condition require a binocular 
Esterman visual field for assessment. This is 
classically done on a Humphrey visual field 
analyser, but any machine that can be shown 
to be equivalent is accepted (e.g. Medmont 
binocular VF printed off in level map mode). 
The treating optometrist or ophthalmologist 
can determine whether it is appropriate for the 
person to wear their normal corrective lenses 
while undergoing testing. Fixation monitoring 
must be performed and recorded on the test.
